content.p: On Friday 27 March 2026, an ordinary "jeans day" at a school in the mining city of Calama, in northern Chile, ended with one school inspector dead and four other people stabbed. The dead woman was María Victoria Reyes Vache, 59, who had worked at the Instituto Obispo Silva Lezaeta for almost 30 years. The suspect was an 18-year-old fourth-year student, an adult in law, who was pulled to the ground by classmates and teachers and handed to Carabineros.

He was charged with qualified homicide and four counts of attempted homicide and has been held in pretrial detention since 31 March. He has not been convicted of anything. No trial date has been reported as of mid-April 2026.

Chile's Carabineros said the call came in at about 10:30 a.m. and the AP reported the attack at about 10:40. Prosecutors say the attacker was detained in flagrante: students and school staff held him until police arrived, and Carabineros then passed him to the PDI, which took over the inquiry.

The account that has emerged comes mostly from La Tercera, which cited investigators, and from the prosecutor's presentation in court. It says the student turned up in black clothing on a day when street clothes were allowed, did not go to class, wandered the grounds and shut himself in a boys' toilet. A classmate told investigators she noticed a yellow reflective vest and something sticking out of his bag under a piece of card, later found to be a sword-like blade. Two inspectors saw that a student had been in the toilet a long time and called him out. La Tercera reported that the PDI believes they saw him come out hooded and wearing goggles, and that he drew a double-edged blade about 30 centimetres long.

Reyes was first. La Tercera and BioBioChile, citing the PDI's findings, say he sprayed her with pepper spray and then stabbed her repeatedly. Other versions differ on the wound. La Tercera, Meganoticias and Notichile say she was stabbed once in the chest; 13.cl, reporting the prosecutor's account at the hearing, says he stabbed her in the back. La Tercera and Notichile place her death in the school yard.

The second inspector, Ayde Moya (spelled Haydée in some reports), was badly wounded when she tried to help. The attacker then moved a few metres to where second-year students were having a music class and wounded three of them, one seriously. Carabineros gave their ages as 16, while 24horas later referred to one seriously hurt student as 15. No minor is named here.

La Tercera said an early police version held that he had first attacked another student over an old quarrel. The regional prosecutor, Juan Castro Bekios, told reporters the inspector was the first victim, and La Tercera noted that all versions agreed the attack was prepared.

One student who had been in a toilet told 24horas that the attacker banged on the door and told him to leave or something would happen to him. Within about half a minute, the student said, the inspector was already dead and others were trying to take the weapons off the attacker. His classmates, he said, then threw the attacker to the floor and beat him until he let go of his weapons.

La Tercera and BioBioChile both say a 15-year-old tackled the attacker and, with help from others, disarmed him, an episode seen in video that 24horas broadcast. Meganoticias reported that a video recorded by students showed the attacker looking calm as school staff held him. BioBioChile said the PDI homicide squad, Carabineros' special-operations unit GOPE and ambulances all went to the school, and that the school evacuated everyone and suspended classes.

The prosecutor said the attacker had two backpacks and that one held a device made to look like a bomb. It contained no explosive but carried a mocking message, which is why GOPE was called. 13.cl, by contrast, listed an "artisanal explosive" among his items and attributed to the prosecution a purpose of distracting pupils. This conflict is unresolved.

Reports listed several knives, a machete-type blade, a retractable baton, pepper spray, solvent, a water pistol that appeared to hold an accelerant, matches, a mask, and, per the student witness, syringes of bleach. Several blades and the baton bore inscriptions with the names of earlier attackers, among them Pekka-Eric Auvinen, the 2007 Jokela school shooter, according to BioBioChile.

Reyes was married, had two children and had worked at the school for almost 30 years, according to Meganoticias. 13.cl, citing the mother of a fourth-year student, said she would have marked 30 years of marriage that June and that her two children, both at university, travelled to the region at once. The mother recalled that she greeted pupils as they arrived with compliments on their shoes and nails, and that her daughter had said the inspector tried to protect pupils and hugged some of them. CNN Chile carried the same account.

Her funeral procession left the school chapel on Monday 30 March and passed her home. Cooperativa said it was to end at La Guaica, where she was to be cremated. 24horas quoted her sister, Catalina Reyes, as saying that the person who caused her death should pay.

Moya's life was reported to be in danger in the days after the attack. Meganoticias said on 16 April that she had been discharged about a month after the attack, while one of its related headlines said she left hospital after two weeks. The two reports do not agree on how long she was in hospital.

Prosecutors and the press named the accused as Hernán Meneses Leal, 18, living with his mother and sister. La Tercera reported that he took about half a million pesos from his mother shortly before the attack and used it to buy weapons and other items. Police searches of his bedroom, according to El Dínamo, turned up a notebook used as a diary, a modified black balaclava and a pack of antidepressants. La Tercera reported that investigators found no computer, only a phone, which was being examined. It also reported that a video titled with the school's name appeared on YouTube in the afternoon, after the attack, under the same username as his other accounts, and was later removed.

His mental health has been a point of dispute. At the 28 March detention hearing, Chilevisión reported, his defence read certificates from a psychiatrist listing level 1 autism spectrum disorder, major depression, panic attacks and a moderate anxiety-depression disorder. On 29 March Castro said that at this stage prosecutors had no serious evidence of a psychiatric condition that would make him not criminally responsible. La Tercera, citing sources close to the case, said he had earlier been diagnosed with severe depression and some degree of autism but that there would be no obstacle to holding him accountable.

A friend told Teletrece, as 24horas reported, that he had been bullied, that nobody was especially kind to him, and that he had struggled after repeating a year. La Tercera noted that no complaints or records backed up the bullying claim. 24horas also reported that days before the attack he had a run-in with a psychopedagogue over his conduct. Parents quoted by La Tercera described him as often alone, dressed in black, with his hair over his face.

On Saturday 28 March the Calama pretrial court held the detention-control hearing, and at prosecutors' request it extended his detention to Tuesday 31 March, so that technical and medical reports could be completed, 24horas said. On 31 March, Meganoticias said, the court granted pretrial detention, agreeing with prosecutors that he was a danger to society and to the victims' safety, and set the investigation period at 180 days. The Clinic gave the day as Wednesday; the other outlets and the scheduled hearing say Tuesday.

Prosecutor Eduardo Peña told the hearing that a notebook seized at the home recorded a plan. As Meganoticias and The Clinic described it, the plan named the attack "Dies Irae" (day of fury) and set a deadline of 15 May. It gave hatred, capitalism and misanthropy as motives, and named first-grade children as the main targets, with anyone who got in his way as secondary targets. It also said he did not expect to survive, hoped to be shot by a police officer, and expected a life sentence if arrested. According to 13.cl, the accused shook his head repeatedly as the prosecutor spoke. The government also announced it would file its own complaint.

On 16 April the appeals court in Antofagasta rejected a petition filed by the defence, which had asked to suspend the proceedings on the ground of mental illness. Meganoticias reported that the court said that remedy was meant for people unlawfully held, and that the accused was not unlawfully detained.

No trial date has been reported, and it is not reported whether prosecutors have closed their investigation or filed a formal accusation. The 180-day period set on 31 March runs on, and the defence's mental-health argument has not been settled by a court.
content.h2: Response, and a wave of threats
content.p: President José Antonio Kast condemned the attack on X and sent his ministers of public security and education, Trinidad Steinert and María Paz Arzola, to the north. Steinert, the security minister, said the government would file a criminal complaint. Arzola told reporters that it was impossible to foresee such an attack at a school without special problems, and said that a school-coexistence law awaiting Contraloría clearance would let schools install metal detectors. Calama's mayor, Eliecer Chamorro, asked for the rules for such detectors to be finished and said the city had gone more than two years without a child psychiatrist. The governor of Antofagasta, Ricardo Díaz, told 24horas, as reported by AP, that nothing of that magnitude had ever occurred in Calama.

On 30 March students from several schools marched to the Silva Lezaeta campus to demand more security, Cooperativa reported, and some also called for justice for Reyes. Notichile reported that the mayor declared three days of mourning.

Fear spread. On 11 April La Tercera cited education ministry figures showing 58 schools had suspended classes over threats since 27 March as of 9 April, 66 with at least eight more the next day. Santiago's metropolitan region had the most cases, with 16, followed by Valparaíso with seven and Antofagasta and Los Ríos with five. Graffiti and posts included a threat to carry out a repeat of the Calama attack. The same report said the ministry planned for the Silva Lezaeta school to reopen on 16 April, citing measures that included self-care sessions and hiring a child and adolescent psychiatrist.

Violence also returned to Calama. On 1 April Radio Agricultura reported that a 12-year-old eighth-grader had been stabbed by a classmate outside a school after a fight. He was out of danger, and the government said it was working on a bill to let schools control what students bring in.
